classification.difficultyReason: Requires a general geometric construction showing that every triangle tiles the plane.

inlines.text: is a tiling of the plane by two-dimensional figures with no gaps and no overlapping (except along edges). Tessellations can involve a single geometric shape, or different types of shapes. If a single shape can be used to form a tessellation, then we say that it tessellates the plane.
Show that any triangle tessellates the plane.

answer.short:
Two copies of any triangle, joined after a $180^{\circ}$ rotation, form a parallelogram.

Translate copies of this parallelogram into rows and stack the rows to tile the plane without gaps or overlaps.
answer.worked:
Rotate the triangle so that one side is horizontal. Rotate a second copy through $180^{\circ}$ about the midpoint of another side. The copies share that side and form a parallelogram: each pair of opposite outer sides is equal and parallel.

Translate copies of the parallelogram along its horizontal side to form a row. Translate the row along the other side to form further rows. These rows cover the plane without gaps or overlaps. Splitting every parallelogram along its original shared side gives a tessellation by copies of the original triangle.

spec.mathematics: Every parallelogram is divided into two congruent triangles related by a half-turn; translations along its two side vectors tile the plane.
